title: Talang Tuo inscription — the Śrīksetra park dedication, 684 CE (Old Malay)
language_note: Old Malay in the Pallava script, stored in the scholarly Latin transliteration, with heavy Sanskrit borrowing in the religious vocabulary — `pranidhāna`, `bodhicitta`, `ratnatraya`, `anuttarābhisamyaksambodhi`. The grammatical frame is Malay and the doctrinal vocabulary is Sanskrit, which is the same mixture seasia-04-dong-yen-chau shows three centuries earlier in Cham.
findspot: Talang Tuo, at the foot of Bukit Seguntang, Palembang, South Sumatra, Indonesia. Discovered 1920.
original_text_excerpt:
swasti śrī śakawarṣātīta 606 ding dwitīya śuklapakṣa wulan caitra sana tatkalaña parlak śrī ksetra ini niparwuat
parwānda punta hiyang śrī jayanāga. ini pranidhānānda punta hiyang sawañakña yang nitanang di sini niyur pinang hanāu ru(-)
mwiya dnan samiśrāña yang kāyu nimākan wūahna, tathāpi. hāur wuluh pattum ityevamadi, punarapi yang parlak wukan
dṅan tawad talāga sawaña yang wuatña sucarita parāwis prayojanākan punyāña sarwwa satwa sacā(?) rācara, waropā yaña tmu
sukha di āsannakāla di antara mārgga lai. tmu muaḥ ya āhāra dṅan āir niminumña sawañakña wuatña huma parlak mañcak mu(-)
ah ya manghidupi paśuprakāra. marhulun tuwi wṛddhi muaḥ ya jāṅan ya niknāi sawañakña yang upasargga. pīdanna swapnawighna. warang wua(-)
tāña kathamapi. anukūla yang graha nakṣatra parāwis di ya. nirwyadhi ajara kawuatanāna. tathāpi sawañakña yang bhṛtyāna.
original_text_note: The first seven of fourteen lines, which is where the dedication and its subject sit; the remaining seven continue the list of benefits sought. The edition's apparatus is kept rather than normalised: `(-)` marks a word broken across a line and `(?)` in line 4 marks a reading the editor was not certain of. PROVENANCE OF THE TRANSLITERATION, stated rather than assumed. The Old Malay is reproduced from the Wikipedia article named in `citation`, which cites Coedes (1930) -- the standard edition -- in its bibliography but does NOT state whose transliteration it prints. The reading of these inscriptions has been established for a century and the text is not in doubt; what is not established is whose transliteration this is, and that is recorded here rather than resolved by attributing it to Coedes. The inscription itself is 7th-century and out of copyright.
notes: NO reference_translation, and that is the record rather than a gap in it. This is a verbatim_machine_english record: the tier PHASE2_PLAN predicted would become the common case and which F3 found, in FINDING 38, to be the hard one. An English translation of this inscription circulates, and it is UNATTRIBUTED -- the article printing it names Coedes (1930) and de Casparis (1975) in a bibliography without saying whose English it prints. That fact REFUSED this text a verbatim_with_provenance slot earlier in this session, because that tier requires a published translation that is CITED, and the same fact QUALIFIES it here: no citable English exists, so resolve_english reaches the passage with `machine` or with nothing, which is the tier's own definition. Coedes published a FRENCH translation; the tier's operative fact is the absence of English, not the absence of translation. THE CONNECTION IS THE ROUTE, and it is stated rather than implied. Srivijaya held the Straits of Malacca -- the chokepoint of the maritime road that carried goods between the Mediterranean and China. This corpus already holds seasia-01-oc-eo-medallion, a gold imitation of a Roman aureus of Antoninus Pius, and seasia-03-khao-sam-kaeo, a Roman intaglio, as find records ON that road. These records are the polity's OWN VOICE on the same road, five centuries later and inside this project's window. The inscription does not mention Rome and is admitted with the reason attached, which is the standard arabia-04-jabal-dabub set. Talang Tuo is the religious counterpart to seasia-06-kedukan-bukit, dated one year later: where that record counts an expedition, this one dedicates a public park and enumerates what its merit is meant to buy — food, water, freedom from disease, and finally `anuttarābhisamyaksambodhi`. Read together they are a polity describing itself in two registers within thirteen months.

findspot_places.note: NO GAZETTEER ID RESOLVED, for the reason recorded on every F3 record: no GeoNames dump is cached here. Bukit Seguntang is a named hill within Palembang and both this record and seasia-06-kedukan-bukit were found on or beside it, about two kilometres apart — a relation NOT encoded here, because proximity is an argument and not a gazetteer fact.
